title: A 22-Year-Old Indian American Just Won the Largest Literary Prize for a US College Student — and She Did It by Blurring Every Genre Line
excerpt: Jaya S. Basu's Sophie Kerr Prize, worth $86,702 — more than the Pulitzer and National Book Award combined — is a milestone for Indian American literary representation.
body:
Jaya S. Basu did not write in one genre. She wrote in all of them — and the judges at Washington College decided that was exactly the point.

The Indian American student has won the 59th Sophie Kerr Prize, the largest literary award for a college student in the United States, worth $86,702. That is more than the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award combined. Her winning portfolio spanned poetry, fiction, nonfiction, and playwriting, all exploring what she describes as "the forces of attraction that govern the universe and act on all bodies."

"As a writer I pride myself on being very multi-disciplinarian," Basu said at the award ceremony at Washington College, Maryland's premier liberal arts institution. "I tried with my portfolio to show how I can blur the lines between genres."

## More Than a Prize

The Sophie Kerr Prize is not just generous — it is singular. Named after an early 20th-century Eastern Shore writer who published more than 20 novels and hundreds of short stories, the award comes from a bequest Kerr left to Washington College with one condition: half the annual proceeds must fund a prize for the graduating senior with "the best ability and promise for future fulfillment in the field of literary endeavor."

Basu was one of six finalists. A theatre and English double major with a creative writing minor, she has already accumulated a striking résumé: her poem "Romance of the Kitchen Sink" won the Spencer Undergraduate Poetry Award Sonnet Prize at West Chester University, and her original play "Mahamoha" — a title drawn from the Sanskrit concept of deep delusion — has collected the Nathan Louis Jackson Playwriting Award, a runner-up Paul Stephen Lim Playwright Award, and a regional nomination for the National Partners of the American Theatre Julie Jensen Playwriting Award.

"Jaya's writing combines erudition and urgency with beauty, surprise, ambition, and purpose," said Sean Meehan, Washington College's associate dean for curricular innovations. "These aren't traits that easily cohere for professional writers let alone undergraduates."

## The Representation Question

Basu herself addressed what her win means in a broader context. "I stand here as one of very few people of color who have won this award at a predominantly white institution," she said. "All of my experiences have shaped me as a person. I'm proud of myself."

For the Indian American community, her achievement sits in a sweet spot of cultural significance. Indian Americans have long been celebrated in STEM fields, business, and medicine — but literary recognition at this level remains rare. Basu joins a small but growing cohort of young Indian American writers who are reshaping American letters: from Rishi Reddi and Avni Doshi to Megha Majumdar and Sanjena Sathian, the literary landscape is changing, but slowly.

What makes Basu's win distinctive is its interdisciplinary ambition. Her play "Mahamoha" draws directly from Indian philosophical traditions, weaving Sanskrit concepts into contemporary American theatre. It is the kind of work that could only come from someone navigating two cultural worlds — and doing so with enough confidence to blur the boundaries between them.

## What Comes Next

The $86,702 prize gives Basu something rare for a 22-year-old writer: time. In an era when young writers often take on adjunct teaching positions or corporate jobs to survive, the Sophie Kerr money is a runway — a chance to write without the immediate pressure of a paycheck.

For NRI parents who have long fretted about their children choosing the arts over engineering or medicine, Basu's win offers a quiet counterpoint. The largest literary prize for a college student in America, it turns out, pays more than many starting salaries in the fields traditionally considered "safe."

Basu, for her part, seems focused on the work itself. Her portfolio suggests a writer who is not interested in fitting neatly into any single tradition — Indian or American, poetic or dramatic, literary or popular. In a country where identity categories can feel both inescapable and insufficient, that might be the most Indian American thing about her.
